Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Dr. Kamal Hossain, M Amirul Islam, Idrisur Rahman and Ms Tanya Amir, Advocates — For the Petitioners. 
Kaiseruddin Ahmed, Deputy Attorney-General (Not argued) — For the Respondents.
parties:
Masdar Hossain (Md) and 440 others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Bangladesh, through the Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
6. In this Writ Petition the petitioners have raised several points including the vires of impugned Orders as contained in Annexure-F and F(1), so far the same relate to the petitioners, on the ground of being violative of fundamental rights of the petitioners as guaranteed by the Constitution. Further point was raised to the effect that inclusion of the Judicial Service with the executive vide Annexure-A to this Writ Petition in paragraph 2(X) as BCS (judicial) is also ultra vires the Constitution. It is their further case that the Subordinate Judiciary under Chapter-II is the part of Judiciary of Part-VI of the Constitution and thereby the Subordinate Judiciary has already been separated by the Constitution. Only the Rules under Article 115 of the Constitution and/or enactment, if necessary, are required to be made for giving full effect to this separation of judiciary. It is further stated that these Judges of the Subordinate Judiciary being Presiding Judges of the Courts cannot be subordinate to any Tribunal and, as such, the petitioners and other Judicial Officers are not subject to the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal in asmuch as the Court cannot be subordinate to the Tribunal. Further, it is stated to the effect that the Assistant Judges and Senior Assistant Judges cannot be deprived of the pays and allowances as they are being given now and in any way they shall not be given lesser benefit in comparison with other officers as prescribed in paragraph 3 of Annexure-F(1) of the Writ Petition till fixation of their pays and allowances and other matters made along with the District and Sessions Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and Subordinate Judges under Article 115 of the Constitution. 

 7. In this case only an affidavit-in opposition has been filed on behalf of respondent No.3 who is the Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Government of Bangladesh, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka, and no other affidavit-in-opposition has been filed. 

 8. This matter came up for hearing on 13-6-96 and on that day this court passed an order requesting the learned Attorney- General to appear in this case as this case involves important questions of law having far-reaching effect. The learned Attorney-General was notified and on 27-6-96 this matter came up in the list and was adjourned on the prayer of the learned Assistant Attorney-General. Again this matter came up for hearing on 29-1-97. On that day, the learned Attorney-General KS Nabi appeared and stated before the Court that he had already written to the Government with respect to the reliefs sought for by the petitioners in the instant Writ Petition and he prayed for some time in order to examine the matter by the government. Since the learned Attorney-General being the highest Law Officer of the Government was praying for time for consideration of the matter by the Government, this Court adjourned the matter up to 24th March, 1997. When this matter was taken up for hearing on 1-4-97, the learned Deputy Attorney-General Kaiseruddin Ahmed informed the Court that the learned Attorney-General has written to the Government expressing his favourable opinion about this case and the Government has not filed any affidavit-in-opposition. Since the learned Attorney-General had given his opinion favourable to the grievances and demands of the petitioners made in this Writ petition, the respondents have not appeared and contested this Rule. In such a situation it appeared to the Court that neither the Government had acted in the meantime in accordance with the opinion of the learned Attorney-General nor the Government is interested to contest this Rule. So, we heard the learned Advocates for the petitioners only in this matter. 

 11. It is their case that since fundamental rights of those judicial officers have been violated by issuing these two impugned orders dated 28-2-94 and 2-11-95, they should be declared ultra vires the Constitution being violative of Articles 27 and 29 guaranteed by the Constitution. We have carefully gone though the impugned orders along with the order dated 8-1-94 vide Annexure-E and it appears to us that some unreasonable conditions were attached with the pay scales of the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges which were not attached in respect of pay scales and allowances of other BCS Cadre holders. In this view of the matter we find that these two impugned orders vide Annexure-F and F(1), so far the same relate to the petitioners and others, are ultra vires the Constitution being violative of the fundamental right Nos. 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Further, no reason has been assigned as to why the benefits with regard to the pays and allowances of those judicial officers were surreptitiously changed to the detriment of their interest although the same were given to them vide paragraph No. 3 of Annexure-E to the Writ Petition. Since the benefits with regard to the scales of pays and allowances of the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges as given in paragraph No. 3 of the order dated 8-1-94 had been abruptly and aribitrarily taken away by the impugned orders vide Annexures-F and F(1) without showing any reason and since that order dated 8-1-94 was, in fact, acted upon and the same created a vested right in favour of the Judicial Officers mentioned above, the impugned portions of the orders vide Annexures-F and F(1) are liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect. At the same time it must also be declared that the re-fixation of pays and allowances with regard to the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges made under Annexur—E dated 8-1-94 stand valid and such benefits given to them cannot be taken away by the authority. It is further held that by ad-interim orders passed by this Court the aforesaid Judicial Officers are continuing to have the aforesaid benefits vide Annexure-E, the same will continue till the new pay scales are fixed in future, by framing necessary enactment and/or rules pursuant to this judgment. 

 12. The petitioners have also challenged the inclusion of the Judicial Officers by paragraph 2 (x) BCS (Judicial) in Bangladesh Civil Services (Re-organisation) Order, 1980, vide Annexure—A dated 1st of September, 1980. It is their case that since the Judicial Service is a separate and distinct service as specified separately in the Constitution under Part-VI, the Judiciary, the same cannot be equated or amalgamated or tagged with the Bangladesh Civil Services in any manner whatsoever. In this connection we may refer to the Constitution of Bangladesh. In the Constitution, Part-IV containing Articles 48 to 64, deals with the Executive. Part-V of the Constitution deals with the Legislature having Article 65 to Article 93. Part-VI of the Constitution comprising Articles 94 to 117 deals with the Judiciary. It has three Chapters of which Chapter-II deals with the Subordinate Courts which, in fact, is the subject matter in the present Writ Petition. It is further contended that Article 136 is a part of Part-IX of the Constitution, that is Services of Bangladesh, and it is in no way connected with the Judicial Service. We find this contention reasonable and valid. Since the Subordinate Courts are part and parcel of Part-VI of the Constitution, the Judicial Officers cannot be equated or tagged with other services. 

 16. ''Relying upon the aforesaid provisions of the Constitution the learned Advocates for the petitioners submit that since the Constitution itself has specified separate and distinct Judicial Service in several Articles of the Constitution and this Judicial Service is a part and parcel of the Part Judiciary as per Articles 114, 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution, it cannot be considered as a part of Bangladesh Civil Service. The term BCS (Judicial) is a fundamental misconception as Judicial Service is recognised and treated separately in the Constitution itself. We find full force in the above submissions of the learned Advocates for the petitioners. In the Order, namely, Bangladesh Civil Service (Reorganisation) Order, 1980, the Judicial Service has been made a part of the Bangladesh Civil Services vide paragraph 2(X) of that order dated 1-9-80. It appears that Bangladesh Civil Services have been dealt with by the Constitution under Part—IX with the heading "Services of Bangladesh", and since the Judicial Service has been specifically mentioned in Articles 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution and defined separately in Article 152(1) thereof, we hold that such inclusion of the ''judicial service'' under the Bangladesh Civil Service vide paragraph 2(x) of the aforesaid Bangladesh Civil Service (Reorganisation) Order, 1980 dated 1-9-80 as BCS (Judicial) is ultra vires the Constitution. Further, some amendments were made in 1986 with regard to the Bangladesh Civil Services (Reorganisation) Order, 1980, showing BCS (Judicial) Cadre at Serial No.16 which we also find ultra vires the Constitution in view of the provisions of Part-VI and the definition of the ''Judicial Service'' as given in Article 152(1) of the Constitution. 

 18. The learned Advocates for the petitioners further submit that in Articles 61 and 62 vide Chapter—IV of Part—IV of the Constitution, the Defence Services have been specified separately. Similarly, the Judicial Service has been specified in the Constitution under Chapter—II of Part—VI thereof. But the Civil Service, as such, has not been defined in any chapter or part of the Constitution. Rather the Services of Bangladesh have been dealt with in Part-IX of the Constitution. So, the framers of the Constitution had the intention to specify the two services, namely, the Defence Service and Judicial Service in the Constitution separately and in general the framers of the Constitution dealt with the Services of Bangladesh in Part-IX of the Constitution. In such a situation, the Defence Services have been correctly governed by separate Acts and Rules and in the similar way the Judicial Service shall have to be governed by separate provisions of Part-VI of the Constitution and the rules and enactments made thereunder. Since the Constitution itself has dealt with the Judicial Service separately as in the case of Defence Services, it must be given a specific treatment totally different and distinct from the Civil Services. The argument has substance in it and cannot be ignored. 

 20. Explaining these provisions of the Constitution the learned Advocates submit that though these principles are not justiciable under Article 8(2) of the Constitution, they are to be applied for the interpretation of the Constitution. In the instant case the petitioners have not come to enforce any fundamental principle judicially, but they have come for a declaration that judiciary had already been separated by the Constitution itself under Part-VI of the Constitution, namely, the Supreme Court, Subordinate Courts and Tribunals, and that the Respondents should be directed to implement and carry out the mandate of the Constitution in pursuance of Articles 109, 115, 116 and 116A of the Constitution. The petitioners have come before this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution which has empowered High Court Division to direct the persons performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do. In the instant case the High Court Division is competent to direct the Legislature as well as the Executive to perform their functions which these authorities are required to do under the Constitution or any other law. So, it is submitted by the learned Advocates that the bar given under Article 8(2) of the Constitution will not be applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case inasmuch as the petitioners are not praying for enforcement of fundamental principles. Rather they are praying for necessary direction and declaration as provided under Article 102(2) (a)(l)(II) of the Constitution with regard to Articles 115, 116 and 116A read with Article 109 of the Constitution, and urging upon this Court to apply the fundamental principles of State policies, particularly Article 22 of the Constitution, in the matter of interpretation of those provisions. 

 26. It may be noted in this connection that there appears to be some misconception in the mind of some person that since the definition of the expression "Service of the Republic" as given in Article 152(1) of the Constitution refers to all services, posts or offices whether civil or military, and Article 133 thereof also relates to persons in the service of the Republic, persons in the judicial service or the magistrates automatically come within the mischief of Article 133. That conclusion is fallacious and it will become apparent from clear reading of the provisions of Chapter-IV of Part-1V, Chapter-11 of Part-VI and definitions of "judicial service" and "service of the Republic." Article 133 begins with the clause "subject to the provisions of the Constitution." It says that Parliament may by law, or the President, in the absence of such law, by rules, provide for appointment and condition of service of persons in the service of the Republic. As Chapter-IV of Part-IV of the Constitution deals with defence service, this article does not apply and has never been applied to such services. Similarly, as Chapter-11 of Part-VI of the Constitution deals with subordinate judiciary and matters relating to appointment and conditions of service of persons belonging to judicial service and ''magistrates, Article 133 has no manner of application to them. Further, one should note that the definition given in Article 152(I) of the Constitution is subject to the condition that they shall have the meanings given to them in that article except where the subject or context does not otherwise require. So, since Article 133 applies subject to other provisions of the Constitution and since the definition of "service of the Republic" will apply when the subject or context does not otherwise require, the clear provision of Chapter-II of Part-VI of the Constitution will apply to Judges and magistrates of the subordinate judiciary and these provisions will over-ride Article 133 in that regard. They are not persons in the service of the Republic for the purposes of Article and hence their appointment or conditions of their service can not be governed under that Article 133 of the Constitution. 

 27. In this connection the learned Advocates for the petitioners have referred to the case of All India Judges'' Association vs. Union of India (1991) I SCC 119. In the aforesaid case the separation of the judiciary, namely, the Subordinate Courts as well as the terms, conditions, benefits of the Judges and all other things relating thereof were subject matters before the Supreme Court of India. 

 28. In that Writ Petition reliefs were sought for by the Judges of the Subordinate Courts for bringing uniformity in the conditions of service for members of the subordinate judiciary throughout the country. Articles 32, 234 and 245 of the Constitution of India were the subject matter for consideration by the Supreme Court. In Article 235 of Indian Constitution provisions were made for controlling over the Subordinate Courts, and control and supervision were vested in the High Court. In that case the Supreme Court ultimately gave directions to the government in the judgment in the following terms: 

 30. In this connection we may also refer to the celebrated judgment of our Appellate Division, namely, Anowar Hossain Chowdhury vs. Bangladesh, reported in 1989 BLD (special issue), I, which is popularly known as ''8th Amendment Case." In this case exhaustive arguments were advanced by the learned members from the Bar and the learned judges also separately dealt with those submissions in that judgement. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed (as he then was) observed that if by exercising the amending power people''s sovereignty is sought to be curtailed it is the constitutional duty of the court to restrain it and in that case it will be improper to accuse the court of acting as super legislators. Supremacy of the Constitution as the solemn expression of the will of the people, Democracy, Republican Government, Unitary State, Separation of Powers, Independence of the Judiciary, Fundamental Rights are basic structures of the Constitution. There is no dispute about their identity. In this judgment the learned Judge further observed that separation of powers and independence of judiciary are the two basic structures of the Constitution. It appears to us that independence of judiciary will not be completed if the judiciary is not separated from the executive. Since in the aforesaid judgment this separation of judiciary and independence of judiciary have been described as being basic structure of the Constitution, the same cannot be taken away in any manner whatsoever. In the instant case, the separation of judiciary, namely, separation of the Subordinate Courts from the executive organs has already been provided for in Articles 115, 116 and 116A, read with Article 109, of the Constitution and this separation of judiciary and the independence of judiciary being the fundamental structure of the Constitution, the same cannot be touched in any manner whatsoever. 

 31. In this connection we may also refer to a case, namely, Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.4927 of 1996 (Contempt of Court) The State vs. Shafique Rehman. This is an unreported case. In this case judgement was delivered on 10-12-96 by a Division Bench of this court. In that case some newspapers including one weekly Bengali newspaper the Jai Jai Din made some criticism of the lower courts with regard to granting bail to former president Hossain Mohammad Ershad. In that connection this court issued a suo motu Rule for contempt of court on the Editor of the Bengali weekly journal the Jai Jai Din. In that case also Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed as well as Dr Kamal Hossain, the learned Advocates, appeared and made their valuable submissions before the court. In that case also this question of separation of judiciary and independence of judiciary were argued by the learned Advocates. Referring to Article 7(2) and also Article 22 of the Constitution it was observed by the Division Bench that in considering the fact that the principles of State policy though not judicially enforceable like the fundamental rights, Article 22 is very much a part of the Constitution which is nothing but the solemn expression of the will of the people. Had it been enforceable like fundamental rights by the court, the court would not hesitate to pass a decree or make a declaration or direction for its implementation and fulfilment, as a long period of 25 years has already passed from the date of independence of Bangladesh. This Article No.22 was not meant for beautifying the Constitution as an ornament, but the will of the people was intended to be implemented within a reasonable time and this period of 25 years from independence is definitely a reasonable period to implement the cherished will and desire of the people. Absolute trust and faith in the Almighty Allah shall be the basis of all actions which is one of the fundamental principles of State policy as per Article 8 of the Constitution. This faith demands that we all should be true to our promise and Article 22 of the Constitution should be implemented in letter and spirit in no time. Since silver jubilee of our independence is being observed throughout the country and abroad, it is high time to show honour and respect to the solemn expression of the will of the people by ensuing separation of judiciary from the executive organs of the State as per Article 22 of the constitution. It is now the solemn duty of all of us particularly the people who are running the affairs of the State to do it. 

 32. In that case also the speech delivered by Hon''ble Prime Minister of Bangladesh on 3-12-96 in Bangladesh Civil Service BCS (Judicial) Association, the 16th conference, had been quoted from the Bengali newspaper the Daily Ittefaq in the following manner. 

 33. In the case of Andhra Pradesh vs. Diksitulu, AIR 1979 (SC) 193 the Supreme Court of India considered Article 285 of the Indian Constitution with regard to control of the High Court over subordinate judiciary. Their Lordships held that the control over the subordinate judiciary vested in the High Court under Article 235 is exhaustive in nature, comprehensive in extent and effective in operation. It comprehends wide variety of nature. In the case of State of Assam vs. SN Sen, AIR 1972 (SC) 1028, Indian Supreme Court discussed the scope of Article 235 of the Indian Constitution with regard to control of the High Court over the subordinate judiciary. In AIR 1993 (SC) case, their Lordships clearly held that judiciary is above administrative executive. There cannot be link between service conditions of Judges and those of the members of other services. 

 38. Article 22 provides that the State shall ensure the separation of the judiciary from the executive organs of the State. The word ''ensure'' is important for the purposes of this case. The ordinary Bengali meaning of the word ''ensure'' is নিশ্চিত করা বা নিরাপদ করা and Constitution''s Bengali meaning is নিশ্চিত করকরা. It means that the State shall see to it that the judiciary is kept separate from the executive organs. It urges upon the State to provide for all matters and to take all measures and steps that may be found necessary to ensure such separation. In other words, the State is required to give all logistic support for ensuring such separation, if necessary, appropriate laws are to be made. But this does not call for constitutional amendment. Constitution has already provided for separation of judiciary from the executive. What is now expected of the State is giving effect to and implementation of the Constitutional provisions in their true perspective. 

 41. Article 115 provides that the appointment of the aforesaid judges and magistrates will be made by the President in accordance with the rules made by him. Such appointment includes all other matters relating to their service conditions. In this connection we may refer to the case reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 193. In paragraph 27 of the judgement their Lordships elaborately discussed the meaning and scope of ''appointment'' which runs as follows: 

 48. Another aspect of the case should be considered with due seriousness. Everybody in the country is speaking about independence of judiciary which is reflecting from Article 116A of the Constitution also. It is a must and it should be a must to make the judiciary fully separate from the executive in all respects in order to attain the cherished goal of all—that is—the "Independence of Judiciary''. Without full and effective separation of judiciary, it is an impossibility to secure and achieve independence of judiciary and guaranteeing individual liberty. The present Government is also preaching highly about independence of judiciary in our country. What is expected of it now is serious early steps for effective completion of separation of judiciary from the executive should be taken in pursuance of this judgement. 

 52. Either in Annexure-E, that is, the Services (Pays and Allowances) Order, 1991 or in Annexure-F(1), that is the amended impugned order dated 2-11-95, the authority is quite silent about the Assistant Judges and Senior Assistant Judges. The impugned orders only relate to subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges. But it appears that they are getting their salaries and other allowances as decided by the government. Let them continue to have the salaries and allowances and other benefits as they are getting now and they should not be given anything below the pays and allowances as specified in paragraph 3 of the impugned order Annexure-F(1) dated 2-11-95 till the framing of the Rules and/or any other enactment as required under the Constitution as per our above findings. Till completion of separation of judiciary the Assistant Judges and Senior Assistant Judges will be having their existing pays, salaries and allowances and/or other ancillary benefits as they are getting now. When the appropriate rules and/or enactment will be framed, their cases will be considered along with the Subordinate Judges, Additional District and Sessions Judges and District and Sessions Judges together. 

 54. We have already stated above that the Government is not contesting this Writ Petition. Further, we are informed by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that, in fact, the learned Attorney-General has given his opinion to the Government in favour of the grievances and demands of the petitioners in accordance with the Rules issued in this case. So, no State lawyer made any argument against the prayers made in this Writ petition. Since Government is not contesting, it is presumed, the Government has no objection if the Rule is made absolute and the prayers made by the petitioners in this Writ Petition are granted.
